Chapter Two: The Imago—How Childhood Shapes Adult Love.
Let’s take a closer look at something that really helps explain why we keep running into the same issues in relationships—the idea of the “imago.”
Imagine this: deep down, every one of us carries an internal picture of what love should feel like. We don’t make this list on purpose; it’s built from our earliest experiences with the people who raised us—mom, dad, or whoever our main caregivers were.
The imago is like a hidden template, quietly guiding who we’re drawn to, and what we expect from love as adults.
Here’s how it works. As kids, we soak in both the good and the difficult moments with our caregivers. So, if you had a parent who could be super loving, but also unpredictable, you might find yourself as an adult looking for someone who’s warm, but whose moods are all over the map. Or, maybe one of your parents was distant or overly critical. Without even realizing it, you might expect your partner now to be critical—or to pull away—even if they're not actually doing it.
This inner blueprint doesn’t just shape who we pick; it also affects how we act in relationships. When a partner touches on an old wound, we often react automatically—maybe by pulling away, criticizing, or just shutting down—exactly like we might have done when we were little. These aren’t conscious choices; they’re old survival moves we learned early on.
Think of the imago as the script behind the scenes of your love life. It explains why certain arguments feel so intense, why a tiny comment can suddenly blow up, or why you keep having the same fights over and over again.
But here’s something to pay attention to—the point isn’t to blame our parents or our partners. Recognizing the imago is about seeing ourselves and each other with a little more compassion. It’s a chance to step out of those old patterns and do things differently.
So, where do you start? Try reflecting on the qualities—both the positive and the tough ones—of the people who raised you. Notice how those traits might show up in your current relationships. It might feel a little uncomfortable at first, but this kind of honest self-inquiry is where real change begins.
